gcartes.title: Mini-course: generalized maps
gcartes.lead: Six short lessons on the structure of my thesis, an unfolded cube to explore dart by dart, and a quiz to check.
gcartes.figure.alt: Net of the cube: six squares, each with its 8 darts, and the letters a to h of the cube's vertices.
gcartes.figure.caption: The unfolded cube: each segment is a dart, the dot marks its vertex; α0 in black, α1 in red, α2 in blue (between squares next to each other in the net; click a dart to see all its links). The same letter is the same vertex of the cube.
gcartes.figure.start: Click a dart, or use the α buttons to move.
gcartes.noscript: The figure and the quiz are interactive with JavaScript; the lessons read without it.
gcartes.label.counts: Counted as orbits: {darts} darts, {vertices} vertices, {edges} edges, {faces} faces, χ = {euler}.
gcartes.legend: Key: α0 links in black, α1 in red, α2 in blue.
gcartes.step.0.title: The object.
gcartes.step.0.text: Two squares sharing an edge: 2 faces, 7 edges, 6 vertices.
gcartes.step.1.title: Cut by α2.
gcartes.step.1.text: The faces come apart; an α2 link (blue) remembers the edge they shared.
gcartes.step.2.title: Cut by α1.
gcartes.step.2.text: Each face falls into its sides; α1 links (red) remember the corners. The shared edge is now sewn at each of its ends.
gcartes.step.3.title: Cut by α0.
gcartes.step.3.text: Each side splits into two darts; an α0 link (black) joins the two halves. 16 darts and their links remain: that is the G-map.

parbench.title: Benchmarks
parbench.lead: The same curvature, computed by each version on tori from 50,000 to 3.2 million triangles; median time, adjacency already built, copies to the graphics card included.
parbench.machine: Measured on {cpu} ({threads} OpenMP threads on {logical} logical processors), graphics card {gpu}, under WSL 2; median of {runs} runs.
parbench.transfers: On the graphics card, in double precision: {upload} ms copying to the card, {kernels} ms computing, {download} ms back, and {host} ms on the processor (allocations). In single precision the computation alone drops to {floatKernels} ms: this consumer card has 32 times fewer double-precision units than single-precision ones. For a single curvature the copies are what costs: computing on the card pays off when the data stays there.
parbench.float: Single precision strays by at most {error} on an angle defect: enough to show colours, not to check Gauss-Bonnet to the millionth.
parbench.memory: Why OpenMP is not six times faster: the vertex pass reads a lot of memory for little computation, and the bandwidth of this machine under WSL tops out at 5 to 6 GB/s whatever the number of threads (measured); the face pass, for its part, runs 4.5 times faster on 6 cores. With 12 threads, the ones spinning while they wait on the logical cores slow the others down: one thread per physical core is faster here.

topo.chi.title: Euler characteristic of the sublevel set against the threshold: it only changes at critical points.
topo.height.note: Like ParaView's Elevation filter: the mesh is coloured by its height, and the slider keeps only the part under the threshold (the triangles whose three vertices are lower). A point is critical when its lower link (its lower neighbours) is not in one piece: no lower neighbour for a minimum, several pieces for a saddle. Computed by the topology C++ code, in WebAssembly.
topo.label.height.check: Morse theory: minima − saddles + maxima = {sum} = χ.
topo.label.height.sum: Sum of the indices = {sum} = χ (non-manifold vertices included).
topo.pers.title: Persistence diagram
topo.pers.desc: Persistence diagram of the height: each point is a component, a loop or a cavity of the sublevel sets, placed at the height where it is born (across) and the height where it dies (up). Far from the diagonal, a real feature; close to it, noise. On the ∞ line at the top, the classes that never die.
topo.pers.note: Each component (H0), loop (H1) or cavity (H2) of the sublevel sets is born at one critical point and dies at another, or never: the classes that never die are the Betti numbers. The distance to the diagonal, its persistence, tells real features from noise: the slider greys the pairs shorter than the threshold and keeps on the mesh only the critical points of the remaining pairs. Computed by the topology C++ code (boundary matrix reduction over Z/2), in WebAssembly.
topo.label.pers.summary: Above the threshold: {h0} component(s), {h1} loop(s) and {h2} cavity(ies) that die; classes that never die (Betti numbers): {b0}, {b1}, {b2}.
topo.label.pers.hidden: {n} less persistent pairs are not drawn.
topo.label.pers.toolarge: Mesh too large to compute the persistence in the browser (more than {limit} triangles).
topo.pers.cloud: The same diagram as a scatter plot
topo.pers.pick.help: Hover, touch or browse with the keyboard (Tab, then the arrows) a bar, a point or a row of the table: the vertex where the class is born and the one where it dies are circled on the mesh, and the height threshold moves between them.
topo.bars.title: Persistence barcode
topo.bars.desc: One bar per component, loop or cavity of the sublevel sets, from the height where it is born to the height where it dies; an arrow at the edge for those that never die. The dashed line is the height threshold: the bars it crosses are the classes alive at that level.
topo.label.bars.alive: At the threshold: {h0} component(s), {h1} loop(s) and {h2} cavity(ies) alive; {h0} − {h1} + {h2} = χ = {chi}.
topo.label.pick.dies: {dim}: born at vertex #{bv} at height {birth}, dies at vertex #{dv} at height {death}. Both vertices are circled on the mesh, the threshold sits between them.
topo.label.pick.never: {dim}: born at vertex #{bv} at height {birth}, it never dies. This vertex is circled on the mesh, the threshold sits above it.
topo.tour.title: Guided explanation
topo.tour.lead: The height threshold rises step by step; at each step, the class that is born or dies is highlighted.
topo.label.tour.first: The level rises from the lowest vertex: at the first minimum, a component is born. It is the oldest one and will never die: its bar runs to the edge.
topo.label.tour.second: At height {h}, the level reaches another minimum: a second component is born, apart from the first.
topo.label.tour.merge: At height {h}, the level reaches the saddle joining the two components: they merge and the younger one dies, the older survives. The length of its bar, its persistence, is the depth of the pit.
topo.label.tour.loop: At height {h}, at a saddle, the level closes a ring: a loop is born.
topo.label.tour.fill: At height {h}, the level fills the loop: it dies.
topo.label.tour.cavity: At height {h}, at the maximum, the last triangle closes the surface: a cavity is born, the enclosed inside. It never dies.
topo.label.tour.end: The whole mesh is under the threshold. What remains are the classes that never die, the Betti numbers: {b0} component(s), {b1} loop(s), {b2} cavity(ies). The short bars, close to the diagonal in the scatter plot, are noise.
topo.reeb.title: Reeb graph
topo.reeb.show: Show the graph inside the mesh
topo.reeb.desc: Reeb graph seen from the front, height upwards: each arc follows a component of a level set from one node to the next; the dashed line is the height threshold.
topo.reeb.note: Each component of each level set is shrunk to a point: nodes are where they appear, split, merge or vanish, and each arc follows one of them, drawn through the centres of the level sets. On a closed orientable surface, the graph has as many loops as the genus, whatever the direction. Computed by the topology C++ code, in WebAssembly; inside the mesh, made transparent, it is cut at the height threshold.
topo.label.reeb.genus: A closed orientable surface: as many loops as its genus ({genus}).
topo.label.reeb.bound: A surface with a boundary or not orientable: at most b1 = {b1} loop(s).
topo.label.reeb.nodes: Too many nodes to draw the Reeb graph (more than {limit}): a noisy height has thousands.
topo.label.reeb.triangles: Mesh too large for the Reeb graph in the browser (more than {limit} triangles).
topo.label.time: Computed in {t} in your browser (WebAssembly, on the page’s thread).
topo.label.time.read: Read and analysed in {t} in your browser (WebAssembly).
topo.bench.title: Computing times
topo.bench.lead: Measured on a standing torus, best of {runs} runs, on one thread of an {cpu}: native (C++ built in Release by GCC) and WebAssembly (the same code, in Node, as in the page). Produced by projects/topologie/scripts/bench.mjs.
topo.bench.gpu: What about a GPU? It would speed up what is done vertex by vertex or triangle by triangle, independently: the height (one dot product per vertex), sorting the vertices (parallel sort), the lower link of each vertex, and H0 persistence by parallel merges. The boundary matrix reduction, though, handles the columns one after the other (each depends on the previous ones), and the Reeb graph relies, like H0 persistence, on union-finds with unpredictable accesses: a GPU would spend its time synchronising. Yet persistence dominates ({p} for a million triangles natively) and it is the part that suits a GPU least: no GPU version (D49).
topo.bench.limit: Why 32 MB? Before any computing, reading an OBJ of {mb} MB (a million triangles) takes {read} in WebAssembly, on the page’s thread, which stays frozen meanwhile; WebAssembly memory climbs to about 190 MB (750 MB for 4 million triangles), capped at 1 GB by the build and at 4 GB in wasm32, and a phone has less. The limit keeps the wait under two and a half seconds; lifting it would take streamed reading in a Web Worker and more memory (D49). Above {limit} triangles, the page also refuses persistence and the Reeb graph: half a second at that cap.
cross.label.green: {axis}: this axis is already green, the request changes nothing.
